articles.title: In 1889, Switzerland opened the Pilatusbahn after Eduard Locher designed a new rack system that helped trains climb Mount Pilatus at gradients of up to 48%
articles.summary: In 1889, Switzerland opened the Pilatusbahn, a mountain railway designed to climb Mount Pilatus using an unusual rack-and-cogwheel system.
articles.body: In 1889, Switzerland opened the Pilatusbahn, a mountain railway designed to climb Mount Pilatus using an unusual rack-and-cogwheel system. Engineer Eduard Locher developed the system after an earlier proposal using conventional rack technology was considered unsuitable for the mountain’s terrain and economic requirements. The railway opened on 4 June 1889 after construction began in April 1886, with steam-powered cars carrying passengers up gradients reaching 48%. Its original cars combined the engine, boiler, fuel and water storage with the passenger compartment on a single chassis. The railway was electrified in 1937, while its basic driving-gear principle remained unchanged.Why was the original 1873 Pilatusbahn plan considered unsuitableA proposal submitted in 1873 called for a cogwheel railway from Lake Lucerne to the summit of Mount Pilatus using the established Riggenbach system. According to the American Society of Mechanical Engineers, the proposed railway would have had a maximum grade of 25% and a 1,435-millimetre gauge. However, technical and economic considerations meant that this design would have produced a route twice as long as the eventual Pilatusbahn, with rolling stock that was too heavy and curves that were too large for the mountain's terrain.Engineer Eduard Locher then proposed a system specifically designed for Mount Pilatus. The gauge was reduced to 0.8 metres, while the maximum grade was increased to 48%, allowing the route length to be reduced. Instead of placing a conventional rack vertically between the rails, Locher designed a horizontal double rack with its teeth facing each side. Two cogwheels on vertical shafts beneath the car engaged with the rack, while flanges helped keep the system engaged even on the steepest sections.When did construction of the Pilatusbahn begin and when did it openConstruction of the Pilatusbahn began in April 1886, and operations began on 4 June 1889, according to the ASME landmark document. The railway was constructed entirely with private capital because the government did not provide a subsidy for its construction. Locher's system was developed in response to the technical, economic and regulatory conditions surrounding the proposed railway.The original railway used steam-powered cars. ASME states that the cars combined the engine, boiler, water and coal storage and passenger compartment on a single four-wheel chassis. The cars were 11 metres long and weighed 11.6 tonnes when fully loaded. During construction, the steam-powered cars were used to transport workers and materials from Alpnachstad to the work site.How does the Pilatusbahn’s unusual cogwheel system workThe Pilatusbahn's unusual propulsion arrangement was designed to keep the cogwheels engaged with the rack on the steep mountain sections. ASME says the system used opposing horizontal cogwheels engaging with a double rack, while flanges beneath the cogwheels helped guide the car and prevent wind and gravity from lifting it away from the rack. The organisation describes the Pilatusbahn as the world's steepest cog railway, with a maximum grade of 48%.The original steam-powered cars were replaced by electric cars in 1937, with further updates made in 1954 and 1967. ASME states that the driving-gear principle and basic design remained the same in the electric version. The current electric cars use twin motors that also provide dynamic braking during descent. Two original steam cars remain in existence, with one on loan to the Swiss Museum of Transport and the other at the Railway Museum in Munich.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.body: NEW DELHI: Congress leader Pawan Khera on Sunday questioned the Election Commission's response to concerns over Form 6, claiming that the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls was based on a change to the form that could not have been made without amending the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960.Speaking to news agency PTI, Khera said the rules could not be changed without being amended in Parliament and questioned whether the Election Commission had addressed the objections raised by Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi."The 1960 Rules cannot be changed without being amended in Parliament. The biggest point of difference between Sandhu ji and Joshi with Gyanesh Kumar was this, and did we receive the answer to it today?" Khera said.Questions Form 6 changesKhera alleged that the SIR exercise was based on an "illegally changed" Form 6 and questioned the validity of elections conducted in Bengal and Bihar on the basis of the exercise."The entire SIR is based on a Form 6 that was changed illegally. The SIR that arose from that illegal form has also become illegal. The elections held in Bengal and Bihar based on that illegal SIR have also become illegal. Did we get an answer on this?" he said.What is the Form 6 row?The controversy centres on the requirement for new voters to provide details linking themselves or their parents or grandparents to electoral rolls from the previous SIR.According to Indian Express reports, Election Commissioners Joshi and Sandhu had objected to incorporating the requirement into Form 6, arguing that the statutory form could not be altered without an amendment to the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960.The Election Commission, however, has maintained that there was "no change" to Form 6 and that the SIR-related requirement was an additional declaration prescribed under its SIR orders. The poll panel has also said the declaration attached to Form 6 for SIR had been upheld by the Supreme Court.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: ‘Old footage’: Delhi Police fact-checks viral Jantar Mantar protest video amid SIR row
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Delhi Police has debunked viral visuals of a massive protest being shared on social media, citing that it contains old footage from Jantar
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Delhi Police has debunked viral visuals of a massive protest being shared on social media, citing that it contains old footage from Jantar Mantar. They have also warned that legal action could be taken against those deliberately spreading misleading content.A video is currently being circulated on social media as showing a live, massive protest against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar. The video was shared by several accounts on X, including Shiv Sena (UBT) MP Sanjay Raut, who claimed that protests against Kumar had begun in Delhi.Raut had shared the video with a caption saying, “Protests against Gyanesh Kumar Hatao have begun in Delhi, today's Jantar Mantar scene... A fight to the finish!”The DCP New Delhi account on Saturday called the claim “false” and said the footage was “archived material from a past event”.“The claim of a live, massive protest at Delhi's Jantar Mantar today is false. The Video is Old: The footage being shared is archived material from a past event,” the Delhi Police said in a post on X.The police also warned that legal action would be taken against those found deliberately spreading misinformation or circulating misleading content.The video surfaced amid a widening political row over the Election Commission’s Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and demands for Kumar’s resignation.The controversy intensified after a report said Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had raised objections at least 14 times over 10 months on decisions and procedures linked to the SIR exercise.Opposition parties have questioned the conduct of the revision and alleged irregularities, while the Election Commission has rejected the allegations.The Election Commission said on Saturday that decisions taken on SIR, including the nationwide exercise, were approved unanimously by the three-member poll panel. It also clarified that a letter sent to the Cabinet Secretary concerned the functioning of an officer on deputation and was not related to any policy decision of the Commission.The poll panel also announced measures to ease the process for voters who receive notices over discrepancies, including allowing booth-level officers to visit their homes to collect documents and providing online hearings in exceptional cases. It said voters left out of the rolls, as well as young and first-time voters, can seek inclusion through the continuous updation process.Protests over SIR rowThe clarification over the viral video comes as opposition-led protests against the Election Commission have continued.The Indian Youth Congress marched from Raisina Road to Jantar Mantar on Friday as part of a nationwide programme demanding Kumar’s resignation. Meanwhile, Peoples Democratic Party chief Mehbooba Mufti has called for a protest at Jantar Mantar on September 29, asking people to join a demonstration centred on democratic and secular values.The Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) has also threatened nationwide protests from October 2 if Kumar does not resign. CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke said the agitation would begin in Mumbai on Gandhi Jayanti and then move to other cities.Opposition parties are also expected to discuss the SIR exercise and the functioning of the Election Commission at an INDIA bloc meeting on September 30.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: At least 27 people killed in two shootings in South African townships
articles.summary: Incidents in Wedela southwest of Johannesburg and Lwandle near Cape Town come days after Durban mass shooting.
articles.body:
At least 27 people have been killed and more than 20 wounded in two shootings in two South African townships, according to police.

In the first incident late on Saturday, at least 17 people were killed and 15 wounded in a shooting at a tavern in Wedela southwest of Johannesburg.

Police said they were searching for eight suspects, who were “reportedly armed with AK-47 rifles and pistols”. The motive for the shooting remained unknown, and no arrests were announced.

Early on Sunday, gunmen killed at least 10 people and wounded 11 at a store in Lwandle near Cape Town.

The shootings took place just days after a shooting at a house party near the city of Durban killed 11 people, including a pregnant woman.

In the first incident, police said the attack began about 9:30pm (19:30 GMT) on Saturday in Extension 3, Wedela, in Gauteng province’s West Rand district.

The gunmen fired at people gathered outside the tavern before going inside, where more shots were fired. Investigators said some customers were searched during the attack and had their mobile phones taken.

The suspects then escaped in two vehicles. Two other vehicles were burned during the incident.

Captain Tintswalo Sibeko said detectives and specialist police units had been assigned to identify and find the eight suspects, with police opening 17 murder cases and 15 attempted murder cases as well as two cases related to property damage.

In the second incident, police said they were searching for multiple suspects after the shooting that took place after midnight on Sunday.

South Africa records persistently high levels of violent crime, including killings involving firearms.

The government has faced sustained pressure to improve public safety, particularly in major urban areas where police have carried out additional operations against gun crimes.

articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Uttar Pradesh chief minister Yogi Adityanath defended the Election Commission amid the \"dissent within the poll body\" row, while slamming the
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Uttar Pradesh chief minister Yogi Adityanath defended the Election Commission amid the "dissent within the poll body" row, while slamming the Congress party for "creating confusion and targeting constitutional institutions".Tearing into the rival Congress for criticisng the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, the Uttar Pradesh CM said: "The current SIR exercise was not the first such revision undertaken by the Election Commission, pointing to similar exercises conducted in 1952, 1957, 1961, 1965–66 and 2003.""Regarding the SIR (Special Intensive Revision), the confusion that has been consistently created by them (opposition parties), it is not as if the current Election Commission is the first to undertake such an exercise; in the past—often under Congress-led governments—similar exercises were conducted in 1952, 1957, 1961, 1965–66, and even in 2003. Despite this history, the uproar raised by the Congress, Samajwadi Party, RJD, and other parties over the current SIR exercise is extremely unfortunate."He said the Election Commission had already clarified that eligible voters who were left out would be given an opportunity to submit the required form. He also referred to the Supreme Court’s position on the Election Commission’s action regarding Form 6."All three Election Commissioners came before the press and clarified the situation. Regarding SIR, directions had already been issued that all eligible voters who were left out would be given an opportunity to fill the form. The Supreme Court has also upheld the Election Commission's action regarding Form 6. Despite this, putting the Election Commission and Chief Election Commissioners in the dock, questioning every constitutional institution and attempting to tarnish India's image globally is extremely unfortunate. Congress and its allies should control their irresponsible actions. There should be no place for violence, vandalism or misinformation in a democracy."Adityanath further accused the Congress and other opposition parties of undermining constitutional institutions and democratic values for political interests."The approach of the Congress and opposition parties has always been to be a part of every conspiracy to harm the constitutional institutions of India and weaken the democratic values ​​for their political interests, due to which the world's largest democracy can be harmed. It is surprising that the current actions and rhetoric of the country's main opposition party and other parties associated with the UPA alliance are extremely irresponsible and damaging to democratic values."Adityanath also criticised the Congress over its objections to EVMs, noting that Congress governments had been formed at the Centre and in several states through elections conducted using the machines. He linked the criticism to what he described as a broader pattern of questioning democratic institutions."The EVMs, through which Congress governments have also been formed at the Centre and in several states, have been called a black box, raising questions about India's electoral system and the country's democratic values. Recall that on June 25, 1975, Congress sinned by undermining the Constitution by imposing the Emergency. Congress-led governments also repeatedly dismissed elected governments of opposition parties through unconstitutional means. Their actions have repeatedly compromised the country's internal and external security. Questioning the valour of the Indian armed forces during the Balakot airstrike and attempting to cast doubt on the bravery of Indian soldiers during Operation Sindoor are examples of this approach."The remarks come amid a major political confrontation over reported objections raised by two Election Commissioners to decisions related to the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. Opposition parties have demanded action against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, an immediate halt to the SIR exercise and fresh elections in states where polls have already been held.The ruling BJP, however, defended the Election Commission, saying differences expressed by Election Commissioners during internal deliberations demonstrated that the poll panel was functioning democratically rather than under a “dictatorial” systemGet the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Avalanche strikes Nepal's Himlung Himal base camp, 10 missing
articles.summary: At least 10 people have gone missing after an avalanche struck the base camp of Himlung Himal in western Nepal, near the Tibet border, expedition
articles.body: At least 10 people have gone missing after an avalanche struck the base camp of Himlung Himal in western Nepal, near the Tibet border, expedition organisers said on Sunday.Expedition organiser Mingma Gyalje Sherpa confirmed that two members of his kitchen staff were among those missing. “The avalanche hit on Sunday morning,” he said, news agency ANI cited.Climbers evacuated after weather warningAccording to Sherpa, expedition and rope-fixing teams had evacuated the mountain slopes after a weather warning was issued last week. However, some people remained at the site despite the worsening conditions.The region had received heavy snowfall for several days, forcing climbers to retreat from autumn expeditions. Those missing in Sunday's avalanche are believed to be associated with different expedition companies.Standing at 7,126 metres in Nepal's Manang district, Himlung Himal is a popular high-altitude climbing destination. Helicopter access to the region requires an additional permit, making rescue operations more difficult.Heavy snowfall disrupts NepalThe avalanche comes as a weather system over the Bay of Bengal brings heavy snowfall to Nepal's mountain regions and persistent rain to the country's hills and plains.Adverse weather conditions have affected several parts of Nepal since Friday, disrupting road connectivity and prompting authorities to close some sections to traffic.The latest disruption follows devastating floods in Rasuwa last month that killed more than 1,400 people and left over 5,000 missing. The floods washed away settlements along the Trishuli River and dealt another blow to Nepal's tourism sector.Persistent rain and snowfall have also disrupted several trekking routes and led to the cancellation or suspension of major expeditions on Manaslu and Dhaulagiri.You use AI every day. articles.title: Archbishop of York sets off on 25-mile Isle of Man pilgrimage
articles.summary: The Most Reverend Stephen Cottrell says there is "massive interest in pilgrimage at the moment".
articles.body:
The Archbishop of York has begun a 25-mile walk on an ancient pilgrimage route across the Isle of Man.

The Most Reverend Stephen Cottrell was joined by the Bishop of Sodor and Man, the Rt Revd Patricia Hillas, and 100 pilgrims.

"There are tears and laughter and beautiful walks," the archbishop told the BBC. "It is very inspiring."

His three-day walk takes place during a weekend of pilgrimage, prayer and worship with churches and communities on the island.

The pilgrims are taking in Triskelion Way, Spooyt Vane Waterfall and Glen Wyllin, as well as walking from Ramsey to Maughold.

On Sunday morning, the archbishop will set off at 10:00 BST from the ancient cathedral within Peel Castle.

The archbishop said: "There is massive interest in pilgrimage at the moment.

"I think it's because in a fast-moving world in thrall to things shiny and new, many of us are looking for something slower and tested by time.

"Pilgrimage can't be hurried. It doesn't happen on a screen."

"The Isle of Man has many ancient places and routes where saints and people of faith have been before us.

"Their faith and lives still shape us today.

"We can encounter the same God today that they knew hundreds of years ago.

"Stepping out, physically or mentally, can take us on a life-giving journey of discovery and encounter."

articles.title: Barkham solar farm construction to start in November
articles.summary: The 43,000 panel solar farm will power 9,400 homes and the council expects it to bring in more than £1m.
articles.body:
Work to build a 43,000 panel solar farm is to begin in November, after a contract was signed with a carbon-neutral developer.

The farm will power 9,400 homes, and will be built on farmland to the south of Barkham, Berkshire, owned by Wokingham Borough Council.

The facility is expected to go live and start generating electricity in September 2027, with full connectivity expected by 2029.

Imogen Shepherd-DuBey, the council's executive member for finance and governance, said signing the contract with Equans was an "important step forward for the council".

She said the the project would also "bring new walking and cycling links, increased biodiversity and hundreds of new trees, creating a lasting legacy for local communities".

The farm is also set to generate more than £1m income for the council every year, according to the authority.

The authority has worked with local charity Freely Fruity to plant about 1,000 fruit trees on the site.

In January, the council said it expected the farm to be built 10 years ahead of schedule.

In 2021, a tenant cattle farmer who worked on the land was told to leave to make way for the solar farm.

Andrew Lake rented High Barn Farm from the council and kept 360 cows at the site.

The authority previously said the land would be returned to agricultural use after 25 years, at the end of the farm's lifecycle.

articles.title: 'I can't afford a house': 25-year-old Gen Z techie earning Rs 1.8 lakh a month says Bengaluru's housing prices have humbled him
articles.summary: A 25-year-old cybersecurity professional earning Rs 1.8 lakh a month in Bengaluru says he was “humbled” by housing prices after discovering that even a Rs
articles.body: A 25-year-old cybersecurity professional earning Rs 1.8 lakh a month in Bengaluru says he was “humbled” by housing prices after discovering that even a Rs 1.3 crore budget may not be enough for the kind of home he wants. For the young professional, buying a home initially appeared to be a realistic goal. Coming from a middle-class family, he said he has always been careful about his spending and does not spend heavily on lifestyle expenses. He chooses to ride a scooter to work instead of buying a car and currently lives alone in a paying guest accommodation. He said his monthly living expenses come to around Rs 31,000. At the same time, he invests Rs 75,000 every month through a systematic investment plan, assuming a return of around 10 per cent, while keeping the remaining amount in his savings account.With his income and relatively frugal lifestyle, he began thinking that a property worth around Rs 1.3 crore could give him a reasonable home. That expectation changed after he contacted a broker and started visiting properties. The man said he looked at homes in Bengaluru's Indiranagar and Whitefield areas and was surprised by what his budget could actually buy. “The problem is, in 1.3 crore, the house I am getting is like a 2 BHK. It is made like a matchbox in some random standalone building, but in a good area,” he said. He also pointed out that larger gated communities can cost considerably more. “The big society, like with 800-900 flats in a gated community, even in Pune, is crossing Rs 2 crore plus like a real good flat,” he said. For someone in his mid-20s, the discovery has raised a larger question about whether a high salary is enough to make home ownership achievable in India's major cities.Should he keep saving or take a loan?The experience has left the young professional questioning whether he should continue living a highly cost-conscious lifestyle for several more years before purchasing a home. “Should I continue living like this on a cost-cutting life for another five years and grow my portfolio and then get some loan to actually afford that expensive house?” he asked. He also said he currently has no plans to get married before turning 30, leaving him more flexibility to focus on building his finances. His dilemma reflects a challenge faced by many young professionals. A salary that may appear substantial on paper can feel very different when compared with property prices in India's major technology and employment hubs.For buyers, the cost of a home is also not limited to the advertised property price. A purchase can involve a substantial down payment, registration and stamp duty, maintenance costs, furnishing expenses and, in the case of a loan, years of interest payments. That makes the decision between continuing to invest and buying immediately particularly significant. At the same time, a Rs 1.3 crore property does not necessarily mean the same thing in every neighbourhood. Location, size, age of the building, amenities and connectivity can dramatically affect prices.gen z getting humbled by housing prices byu/Novus69xD inpersonalfinanceindiaGen Z's housing frustration strikes a wider chordThe young man's experience resonated with social media users, many of whom said buying a home in a major Indian city has become increasingly difficult for younger professionals without substantial savings or family support. One user responded: “A fellow 25M professional here. In my opinion, there's a reason most people buy their house only after 35-40, once they have enough savings.” Another suggested that India's housing market may remain expensive unless there is a major economic disruption. The discussion also reflected a growing generational frustration. One commenter wrote: “It is so damn true. It feels like us, Gen Z and middle-class people, can't even afford a house in big cities. It's for the rich only.”Another user offered a more reassuring perspective, writing: “My heart goes out for Gen Z. As a millennial, I've seen bad times but Gen Z is having a real challenge at hand. But you guys will be fine, you'll figure it out.” The story ultimately raises a question larger than whether one 25-year-old should buy a house now. For young Indians earning relatively good salaries, the traditional milestones of adulthood are increasingly being weighed against soaring urban housing costs. For this cybersecurity professional, the calculation is still open. For now, he has investments, savings and a stable income, but buying the home he considers worthwhile may require more patience, a larger loan or a significant change in expectations. His experience also highlights an important reality: earning well does not automatically mean being able to afford the kind of home you want in India's most expensive cities.You use AI every day. articles.title: Why families are being urged to look closer on autumn walks
articles.summary: Experts urge families to spot, photograph and enjoy autumn fungi on their doorstep.
articles.body:
From fairytale toadstools to fungi that look like birds' nests, experts say some of Britain's most unusual mushrooms are beginning to emerge as autumn arrives.

Hidden in parks, woodlands and nature reserves, species ranging from the bright-red fly agaric to the rare red cage fungus can be found by anyone willing to slow down and take a closer look.

For James Benwell, of the Birmingham and Black Country Wildlife Trust, searching for fungi has become a way to explore the outdoors with his young son.

He said mushroom spotting can transform an ordinary walk into an adventure, revealing colourful and unusual species that many people pass by without noticing.

Across the West Midlands, fungi enthusiasts have recorded everything from tiny bird's nest fungi in Birmingham city centre, to fly agaric mushrooms growing beneath woodland birch trees and a rare red cage fungus discovered in Cannon Hill Park.

Many species can go unnoticed among fallen leaves, rotting wood and the bases of trees, but Benwell said taking the time to look more closely opens up a hidden world.

"Every walk becomes interesting and exciting if you're exploring and if you're looking for new things," he said.

With more than 15,000 species of fungi found in the UK, experts are encouraging people to photograph and record what they find, rather than pick them.

Interest in fungi has grown in recent years, according to Lucas Large, chairman of the West Midlands Fungus Group, who said the organisation regularly attracted newcomers to its activities and fungi forays.

Benwell added one of the attractions was the variety of shapes, colours and forms that can be discovered throughout autumn.

"Sometimes you've just got to look through the leaf litter a bit, and you'd be amazed at the colours and different shapes and sizes of mushrooms you can find when you do look," he said.

Among the most recognisable species is the fly agaric, the striking red mushroom covered in white spots that has become closely associated with folklore and popular culture.

Benwell described it as "the mushroom of fairy tales".

"It's in Alice in Wonderland, it's in Super Mario Brothers... It's everywhere as part of fairy tales and folklore," he said.

"But there are still adults who've never seen it."

Other species offer equally unusual sights. Bird's nest fungi resemble miniature nests complete with tiny eggs, while the rare red cage fungus forms a vivid crimson lattice structure.

The latter was spotted in Birmingham's Cannon Hill Park last year, in what Benwell said was only the second recorded sighting of the species in Birmingham and the Black Country.

"UK-wide, you're only talking hundreds of records ever. It's not a common species at all," he said.

Large said the red cage fungus also had another notable characteristic.

"It smells horrible," he said, explaining the fungus attracts flies which help spread its spores.

After more than a decade studying fungi, Large said the rarest species he had seen in the region was the coral tooth fungus.

"It formed this enormous kind of white, coraloid fruiting body," he said.

While the colourful displays may encourage people to learn more about fungi, experts are warning against assuming wild mushrooms are safe to eat.

Several species found in the UK can cause severe illness or death if consumed, including the death cap mushroom, which the Woodland Trust says is responsible for most fungus-related fatalities.

Large said there was no foolproof shortcut to determining whether a mushroom was poisonous.

"The only way to do it is to know which one it is, or be sort of certain that you've got a particular species," he said.

Benwell agreed and said people without specialist knowledge should avoid picking wild mushrooms.

"There are mushrooms that will harm you, that will make you sick or even kill you in this country," he said.

"The best place to get your mushrooms if you want to eat them is the supermarket."

Instead, people are encouraged to enjoy fungi where they are found, whether in Birmingham city parks, the woodlands of Cannock Chase, Sutton Park or the Wyre Forest.

For Benwell, that approach allows families to enjoy the excitement of discovery while ensuring the region's remarkable fungi can be appreciated by everyone who passes by.

articles.body: A 1962 Missouri house bought by Michael and Lisa Willhoit in 2013 has been transformed into the “African Queen”, a highly unusual retreat with a 15-foot Zulu warrior sculpture, a 20,000-piece crocodile mosaic and interiors filled with materials sourced from different parts of the world. The Springfield property is now on the market for $1.2 million.According to Realtor, the African Queen is a 3,176-square-foot home designed by Don Russell in 1962. The property sits on four acres in Springfield and is built directly above spring-fed water, with ponds, a creek, waterfalls and gardens spread across the grounds.The home has been used as a short-term rental and is currently listed as an active property. The listing says it could continue as a private residence or be used as a hospitality destination or a “healing nature retreat”.Much of what makes the house unusual is inside. The property has monumental doors sourced from India, reclaimed 18th-century Indonesian teak and light fixtures made using ostrich eggs and gemsbok horns. Its floors also include an intricate wood mosaic made from oak, walnut and ebony.A house filled with unusual detailsThe mosaic floor was created by New York City-based Archetypal and contains approximately 550,000 pieces of wood, according to the current listing. Among the artwork is a 20,000-piece crocodile mosaic.The house also has four-inch Carthage stone countertops and a wood-burning fireplace with an indoor grill. One of its more unusual features is a two-inch-thick glass floor that looks directly into the spring-fed water below the house.The natural setting continues into the home through its bluff room, which is built into the surrounding rock. The room has a custom copper hot tub and adds to the property's connection with the landscape.The primary suite has two balconies, a fireplace and a sitting area, along with a 260-gallon aquarium. Its bathroom has sinks made from 1,000-year-old petrified wood and an oversized walk-in shower. The guest bathroom has a hammered copper soaking tub.The 15-foot Zulu warriorOutside the house, one of the most visible features is a 15-foot Zulu Warrior sculpture by Tom Ehlers and James Hall. The sculpture stands on an island on the property and is one of the details that has helped give the African Queen its distinctive identity.The grounds cover about four acres and include spring-fed ponds, a creek, waterfalls and mature gardens. The current listing also mentions wildlife on the property, including a family of otters.The house's design was intended to work with its natural surroundings. Its water views and outdoor landscape are visible from the living spaces, while features such as the glass floor connect the interior directly to the spring-fed water beneath the home.A $1.2 million Springfield listingThe African Queen is currently listed for $1.2 million. The property has two bedrooms and two bathrooms and covers 3,176 square feet. It was added to the market about 15 days before the Saturday's listing update.The Coldwell Banker listing describes the home as an architectural icon in Springfield's Brentwood area and says it has become one of the Ozarks' recognisable residences.The African Queen was also the No. 1 property on Realtor.com's list of the week's most popular homes. Its combination of unusual architecture, elaborate interior details, water features and the large Zulu warrior sculpture has made the 1962 house stand out among other properties recently attracting attention.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Burnham-on-Sea church marks 200 years of historic angel statues
articles.summary: St Andrew's Church is marking 200 years since the angels with a royal past came to Somerset.
articles.body:
A Somerset church is celebrating 200 years since a group of angel statues with links to kings, queens, Sir Christopher Wren and Westminster Abbey, arrived in the county.

St Andrew's Church in Burnham-on-Sea, has been marking the anniversary with a series of community events, culminating with a rededication and blessing service later.

The 17th Century sculptures once formed part of King James II's altarpiece at Whitehall palace and survived a palace fire and political upheaval, before being brought to St Andrew's in 1826.

The Reverend Cheryl Hawkins, Vicar of Burnham-on-Sea Benefice, said the anniversary has given the church an opportunity to bring the community together.

The angels originally formed part of an altarpiece commissioned by King James II for a chapel at Whitehall Palace.

Acclaimed English architect, Sir Christopher Wren, designed both the chapel and the altarpiece.

The carvings are thought to have been been completed around Christmas 1686, just two years before King James II was deposed.

Due to the association with the Catholic king, the altarpiece was dismantled and taken into storage, which proved fortunate as a few years later, most of Whitehall Palace was destroyed by fire.

The altarpiece spent around a century at Westminster Abbey before being removed again and the surviving pieces eventually being brought to Burnham-on-Sea.

To celebrate the anniversary, the church has held a series of events, including an angel-themed trail for families, children's events, a prayer installation and a project which has seen parishioners create scores of knitted angels.

Community groups and local schools are invited to take part in the main celebrations through angel-inspired artwork and music.

Hawkins said: "We hope it will encourage people to step inside our lovely church, perhaps for the first time, and discover all that the church has to offer.

"Its history and beautiful surroundings, our spaces for prayer and reflection, and to experience the warm welcome from the people who are part of St Andrew's Church community today."

articles.title: Psychology says parents who repeat childhood traditions may be shaping their children’s identity and sense of belonging
articles.summary: A father takes his children to see Christmas lights because his own father once did the same with him.
articles.body: A father takes his children to see Christmas lights because his own father once did the same with him. A mother prepares the birthday breakfast she remembers from childhood. Another parent continues a holiday ritual, reads the same bedtime story or returns to a family vacation spot that has been part of their memories for decades. At first glance, these actions may look like simple nostalgia. But psychology suggests that family traditions can carry something much deeper. They can preserve memories, communicate family values and create a sense of identity and belonging that connects one generation to the next. Research on intergenerational transmission shows that some parenting behaviours can be influenced by experiences people had while growing up. A recent meta-analysis found that parenting practices show modest intergenerational stability, meaning that people may carry some aspects of how they were raised into the way they parent their own children. However, this transmission is far from automatic, and many factors can shape how adults ultimately raise their children.Psychology says childhood experiences can shape future parentingOne explanation comes from Social Learning Theory, associated with psychologist Albert Bandura. The basic idea is that people can learn behaviours by observing important people around them, particularly during childhood. That can help explain why a child who grows up watching a parent prepare a particular meal every Sunday may later repeat the same tradition with their own children. The child may never have been explicitly told that the tradition should continue. Instead, the behaviour became familiar through repeated observation. Research on intergenerational transmission of parenting suggests that this process can operate through observation and modelling. Children may absorb aspects of their parents' behaviour and later reproduce some of those patterns when they become parents themselves.But this does not mean people simply copy everything their parents did. The evidence suggests that intergenerational continuity is generally modest and varies depending on the behaviour being studied. Adults can consciously preserve certain practices, change others or reject traditions they did not find helpful. That makes family traditions especially interesting. A parent may recreate the warm experiences of childhood while deliberately avoiding the parenting styles they disliked.Family rituals can become part of a child's identityPsychologists also distinguish between family routines and family rituals. A routine usually helps organise everyday life, while a ritual carries additional emotional or symbolic meaning. Eating dinner at a particular time because everyone needs to eat is a routine. Preparing a grandmother's recipe every Sunday while sharing stories about relatives can become a ritual. A major review by psychologist Barbara Fiese and colleagues examined five decades of research on family routines and rituals. The researchers distinguished routines as observable practices from rituals as symbolic representations of shared family events. They also found associations between family routines and rituals and areas such as parenting competence, child adjustment and family relationships, while noting limitations in the existing research.This symbolic element may explain why certain traditions survive even when they are no longer practically necessary. Consider a parent telling a child, “My father used to take me here when I was your age.” The outing is no longer simply a trip. It becomes a connection between the child's present, the parent's childhood and the grandparent's role in the family story. Research on family mealtimes has similarly explored how routines and rituals can provide structure while helping families create a sense of identity and emotional connection.Repeating a tradition can tell children where they belongFamily traditions do not have to be elaborate. They can be as small as making pancakes on Sunday morning, taking the same photograph on the first day of school or watching a particular film every year. For children, repeated experiences can create predictability. Over time, these small rituals can become associated with feelings of home, family and belonging. The same tradition can also carry different meanings for different generations. A grandmother may have prepared a particular dish because it was part of her family's culture. Her daughter may continue making it because it reminds her of childhood. Her grandchildren may eventually associate the same food with family gatherings and their own childhood. In that sense, the tradition has travelled across generations while its meaning has continued to evolve. Psychology does not suggest that every repeated family habit is automatically beneficial. Nor does continuing a childhood tradition mean that a parent is unable to move beyond the past. Families change, and traditions can be adapted to fit new circumstances.What matters is the meaning attached to them. A parent can preserve a Sunday family meal while changing the recipe, location or format. They can continue a holiday tradition while creating new ones of their own. They can keep the parts of childhood that brought warmth and belonging while leaving behind practices that caused harm. Ultimately, when parents pass a tradition to their children, they may be passing down more than an activity. They may be handing over a memory, a family story and a small piece of identity. Sometimes, a simple sentence such as “My parents used to do this with me” is really another way of saying, “This was important to me, and now I want it to become part of your story too.”You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2012, Pinzón Island began eradicating invasive rats; nine years later, scientists found 156 wild-born young giant tortoises, though recovery still needed support
articles.summary: After eradicating invasive black rats, Pinzón Island has seen a resurgence in its giant tortoise population, with 156 young tortoises born and an estimated 1,100 tortoises now living in the wild. Discover how conservation efforts are revitalizing this unique ecosystem.
articles.body: In December 2021, a team of 24 scientists and park rangers spent 10 days counting giant tortoises on Pinzón Island in the Galápagos, nearly a decade after black rats had been removed from the island. According to the Galápagos Conservancy's release on the census, they estimated the island's Pinzón giant tortoise population at between 975 and 1,100 and located 156 juveniles that were all born after the rats were gone. According to the Conservancy, the number of tortoises on the island was increasing for the first time in a century. However, the Conservancy cautioned that the population was still not self-sustaining.Before 2012, fewer than 200 adults remained, and no hatchlings survived in the wildAccording to the Galápagos Conservancy, black rats were introduced on Pinzón Island in the late 1800s and ate tortoise eggs and baby tortoises; hence, there was no natural reproduction for over a century. A 2018 paper published in PLOS ONE reported that, before the rats were removed, the Pinzón giant tortoise (Chelonoidis duncanensis) faced extinction, with fewer than 200 adults remaining and no juveniles surviving because of the invasive black rats. Because no baby tortoises survived in the wild, conservationists collected eggs from natural nests, raised the hatchlings in captivity, and released the juveniles back into the wild. According to the Galápagos Conservancy, the first 20 juvenile Pinzón giant tortoises were released in 1970, and by the end of 2017, a total of 1,007 had been repatriated to the island.Rat eradication began in December 2012 The rat eradication program took place in December 2012, with Island Conservation, the Galápagos National Park Directorate, and other collaborators. A year later, when the island was declared rat-free, it became the largest Galápagos island where rats have been successfully eradicated. The program also left residual rodenticides in some lava lizards.The first hatchlings emerged on Pinzón by December 2014The first tortoise hatchlings were noted to have emerged by December 2014 from their nests. As stated by the Conservancy, these are the first hatchlings and the first survival of baby tortoises on the island of Pinzón in almost a century. According to another Conservancy report, natural recruitment into the wild population has gone on ever since.A 2021 census recorded 156 juvenile tortoisesThe survey was organized by Wacho Tapia, the Conservancy's Director of Conservation, as part of the Iniciativa Galápagos initiative conducted in conjunction with the Galápagos National Park Directorate. As of 2017, the island held 100 native individuals and 400 of the repatriated tortoises, ranging from 5 to 40 years old. The 156 juvenile tortoises represent the group that indicates natural reproduction is taking place. This survey was a field study announced in the Conservancy release, not a peer-reviewed study.A 2018 genomic study compared 25 historical and 149 modern samples A separate peer-reviewed paper examined the same tortoises from a genetic angle. In a 2018 study in Evolutionary Applications, Jensen and colleagues compared genome-wide DNA from 25 historical museum samples, collected on an expedition in 1905 and 1906, with 149 contemporary samples, collected around 2014. The estimated effective population size of the current generation was 58, with a 95% confidence interval of 50 to 69.It was established that genetic diversity between modern and historical specimens was basically identical, with no traces of genetic patterns associated with a population bottleneck being observed, as well as the absence of population structure. The estimated effective population size of the current generation was 58, with a 95% confidence interval of 50 to 69. This number reflects the number of reproductive individuals within a population and thus cannot be considered a census number. In conclusion, the authors assert that head-starting saved the Pinzón giant tortoise from impending extinction. However, since the modern specimens were collected around 2014, roughly two years after the rat eradication program, this study essentially provides information regarding the genetic characteristics of the population after years of head-starting, but not regarding the juveniles recorded in 2021.Egg collection at the Fausto Llerena Center was still recommended after the 2021 censusThe Conservancy recommended continuing to collect eggs and bring them to the Fausto Llerena Giant Tortoise Breeding and Rearing Center, where the eggs are incubated and hatchlings are kept until they reach five or six years of age. The whole island has recovered as well. Tapia noted that the ecosystem now provides better conditions for endemic species of flora and fauna, including hawks, Galapagos rails, finches, and lizards, and trees like yellow cordia, carob, and cat’s claw. Danny Rueda, the Director of the Galapagos National Park, said that ten years after the eradication, the tortoise population could be positively identified as recovering.You use AI every day. articles.title: Bolton make-up artist condemns the ugly side of social media
articles.summary: Mitchell Halliday was shocked by "vile" comments left on a recent video featuring his client Katie Price.
articles.body:
A make-up artist and beauty brand founder has condemned "cruel" online trolls who flooded his social media accounts after he came up with a red carpet look for reality star Katie Price.

Mitchell Halliday, who created the make-up brand Made By Mitchell and has worked with the likes of Kim Kardashian, received tens of thousands of comments on a video of the makeover, some of which he said were "too vile" to repeat.

Halliday, from Bolton, said: "I've seen a lot of social media so it doesn't really shock me anymore - but the women talking about Katie struck me.

"Some of it was just so vile and just straight to the attack."

Price, who rose to fame as model Jordan in the late 90s, has been vocal about her body dysmorphia and cosmetic procedures.

"I've not really ever seen this amount of cruelty before," said Halliday, whose previous online content has been shared by Kardashian and celebrity make-up artist Makeup by Mario.

"It's almost like people think that we're not going to see the comments.

"Katie loved the look and knowing I made her happy was all I cared about."

Halliday, who said the episode had made him feel "quite sad", has since posted a video in defence of Price and his brand.

"I was in shock that so much negativity had come to the page that I have nurtured and created such a beautiful community with over the last 10 years.

"I want people to come to my platform and see that people who are doing things differently are celebrated."

He added that he and Price have bounced back from the incident and plan to work with each other again in the near future.

"I don't take things too personally and thankfully Katie doesn't either."

Price declined to comment when contacted by the BBC.

Halliday is no stranger to celebrity collaborations.

In 2018, he was invited to Amsterdam to film with US make-up icon NikkieTutorials.

"The visibility that I gained overnight was insane," he said.

"How the hell does a little kid from Westhoughton end up getting reposted by Kim Kardashian and the most famous make-up artist on the planet?"

Reflecting on what inspired him to become a make-up artist, Halliday said his love of make-up started in school, when he would experiment with drawing on his eyebrows.

"My headteacher was a great man," Halliday said.

"He tried to get me to take them off in the most loving way.

His first job in the industry came after a short stint on ITV's The X Factor, where he briefly appeared as part of boyband No Getaway.

Dropped before the bootcamp stage, Halliday turned his attention to beauty and got a part-time job at a friend's salon in Manchester.

"I've always loved the aspect of transformation and I ended up picking up some brushes and loved it," he said.

Halliday was never professionally trained, but said his time working at the salon meant he was constantly learning and working with some of the best in the industry.

Using those skills, Halliday said he started sharing his looks on social media and quickly began to attract attention.

"It blew up and I was quickly noticed by the biggest names in the beauty industry," he said.

Having founded his brand during Covid, Made By Mitchell became the first in the UK to hit $1m in sales in one day on TikTok Shop - during a 12-hour live event in 2024.

After travelling around the world with his career, Halliday now has an office in Manchester and said he was happy to be "home".

"Did I ever think I would end up where I am now? Definitely not," he said.

"I didn't even think that was possible. Coming from a little council estate in Bolton you don't really see that kind of representation when you're growing up.

"I truly think I've been put on this earth to make people feel great about themselves and to listen to people and to give them the space to be themselves.

"But there's so much more that I want to do."

articles.title: Meta refused to run ads promoting Elon Musk's documentary; calls it 'error and ...'
articles.summary: Facebook's parent company, Meta, initially refused to run paid ads promoting Elon Musk’s upcoming documentary, a report claims.
articles.body: ​Facebook's parent company, Meta, initially refused to run paid ads promoting Elon Musk’s upcoming documentary, a report claims. But now, the social media giant has reversed that decision and is calling the rejection an “error.” The company also confirned that its now restoring the ads. The development came after a report claimed that Meta, TikTok, YouTube and X had all declined to carry ads for the upcoming documentary trailer about the world’s richest person, which is directed by Alex Gibney. The companies reportedly cited rules around political content for rejecting the ads​However, a TechCrunch report now claims that Meta has reversed the decision. A company spokesperson told the publication, “This was an error and the ads are being restored.” The reversal leaves Meta no longer among the platforms blocking the documentary’s promotional campaign, while questions remain over why the trailer was initially classified as political content.​Meta says ad rejection was an error​The Hollywood Reporter first reported that several major social platforms had rejected paid advertising for the trailer of Musk’s documentary. Meta was among the companies that reportedly declined to run the promotion, prompting the film’s US distributor, Bleecker Street, to appeal the decisions.​Later, Meta told TechCrunch that its decision was not intentional. However, the company has not yet provided further details explaining how the trailer was initially flagged or what led to the reversal.​The issue appears to have been connected to platforms’ restrictions on political advertising. Meta restricts political ads in certain markets, while TikTok has said it does not allow political advertising. However, classifying a theatrical documentary trailer as political advertising raised questions because the promotion was for a film, not a political campaign.​YouTube also reverses its decision​YouTube has also clarified its position after the reports emerged. The company said that the Musk trailer had always been available on YouTube as a regular video. However, when it was submitted as a paid advertisement, the platform’s systems temporarily restricted it.​Following a review, YouTube said the advertisement had been cleared to run. This means the platform’s initial restriction was also not a permanent ban on the documentary’s promotional material.​Meanwhile, X (previously Twitter) had also reportedly rejected the advertising. Elon Musk owns the platform and has publicly criticised Gibney, recently writing that “Dogs**t is worth more respect than Gibney.”​What is Alex Gibney’s Musk documentary about​Gibney is known for documentaries including Going Clear, The Inventor and a film about Steve Jobs. His latest project about Musk examines the billionaire’s technology career, personal life and political activities.​The documentary premiered at the Venice International Film Festival earlier this month and is scheduled for a US theatrical release on October 9. It is nearly four hours long and includes interviews with people connected to Musk, including his ex-wife Justine Musk and former right-wing influencer Ashley St. Clair.​The film has also attracted strong early critical attention. It currently has a 100% “fresh” rating on Rotten Tomatoes, according to TechCrunch, while Vulture critic Bilge Ebiri described it as a “fascinating” character study. Ebiri wrote, “As a tale of modern business, it’s revealing. And as a warning about our future, it’s terrifying.”​Documentary faces wider distribution questions​The advertising controversy comes as Musk also faces uncertainty around its international distribution. The Hollywood Reporter previously reported that Universal Pictures had been wavering on its international distribution plans, linking the uncertainty to concerns about angering the Trump administration. Universal later said it would release the documentary in theatres, though it was still working out its broader release strategy.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Leeds Baby Bank calls for more donations to help families
articles.summary: The founder of Leeds Baby Bank says the charity has seen a "massive" increase in referrals recently.
articles.body:
The founder of a charity which provides essentials like Moses baskets, prams, nappies and clothes to struggling families across Leeds has said it urgently needs more donations to help keep up with demand.

Chantal Nogbou said there had been a "massive increase" in the number of people referred by health and social care professionals to Leeds Baby Bank in recent months.

Nogbou said staff had helped an "unprecedented" 550 families in Leeds since the start of June, and were expecting numbers to rise as winter loomed.

"We get even more people needing help then because they want to put the heating on, but they still need to buy nappies and feed and clothe their child," she said.

Nogbou founded Leeds Baby Bank in 2017 when she was a single parent of four children, including twins, and she realised how many other families were struggling.

The charity will be 10 years old in January and Nogbou said that staff had seen a change in the families who needed their support over time.

"When we started, pre-Covid, maybe one in five children in Leeds lived in relative poverty," she explained.

"Now, you're looking at one in two children in some parts, and that's just a shocking number that really shouldn't be happening."

Nogbou said that about 70% of the children they helped had a parent who was working and she said many were "not managing to manage the bills with energy and fuel prices going up".

According to government statistics, 27% of children in the Yorkshire and Humber region lived in relative low income families - the joint highest proportion, alongside the West Midlands, in the country.

A relative low income family is one living on less than 60% of the median national household income for that year.

Nogbou said the rise in referrals meant more financial challenges for the charity, especially after moving from a city centre office to a larger and more accessible building in Armley which could now provide more services.

"All that has cost money and obviously bills for us have also gone up when it comes to the utilities, so it's definitely a scary thing as a charity," she said.

She added that it was the donations of items and money from the community that had kept the charity going.

"It's the people that, instead of buying a coffee every day, set up a direct debit and send £5 to Leeds Baby Bank every month," she said.

"That £5 can buy something like a brand new mattress for a Moses basket."
